core.p: **Part (b)**: Explain the importance of the past **elsewhere in the novella**. In your answer you must consider: how the past is presented; why it is important to Scrooge’s change. You should refer to the context. (20 marks)

essays.q: Explain the importance of the past elsewhere in the novella.
essays.t: Model essay: time, memory and regret
essays.text:
Dickens uses time as the structure of Scrooge’s redemption: the past explains his coldness and awakens regret, but the novella insists that the future is not fixed, so memory becomes the first step towards change rather than a sentence.

Marley introduces the danger of regret that comes too late. He tells Scrooge that ‘no space of regret can make amends for one life’s opportunity misused!’, and the phantoms outside the window, chained and desperate to help the poor, have ‘lost the power for ever’. For a Christian Victorian readership, this vision of the afterlife made the stakes of a selfish life clear: there is a limited time in which to act.

The Ghost of Christmas Past shows how memory can restore feeling. As soon as Scrooge sees the countryside of his childhood, he is ‘conscious of a thousand odours… each one connected with a thousand thoughts, and hopes, and joys, and cares long, long, forgotten!’ The repetition of ‘long’ conveys how deeply these memories had been buried. Seeing ‘a solitary child, neglected by his friends’, he weeps; Dickens, drawing on his own lonely childhood in the blacking warehouse, invites sympathy for the boy. Memory immediately produces regret in the present, as Scrooge wishes he had given something to a carol singer at his door.

The past also reveals choice. Belle tells Scrooge that ‘Another idol has displaced me… a golden one’ and that he fears ‘the world too much’. Dickens shows that Scrooge’s isolation was not simply caused by his unhappy childhood but chosen in young adulthood, when love was replaced by the ‘master-passion, Gain’. When Scrooge sees Belle’s happy family, he begs to be removed, and he tries to extinguish the Ghost’s light: the pain of regret is almost unbearable.

Finally, Dickens shows that the future can change. At his grave Scrooge asks whether the visions are ‘shadows of the things that Will be, or… things that May be, only?’, and vows: ‘I will live in the Past, the Present, and the Future. The Spirits of all Three shall strive within me.’ When he wakes and finds he has not missed Christmas, the time he feared was lost is restored. In Stave 5 his ‘back-payments’ to the charity collector express his wish to repair the past. Dickens’s message to his readers is hopeful but urgent: remember your past, see the present clearly, and act before the future becomes fixed.
essays.thesis: Dickens uses time as the structure of Scrooge’s redemption: the past explains his coldness and awakens regret, but the novella insists that the future is not fixed, so memory becomes the first step towards change rather than a sentence.
why: **AO1**: a nuanced thesis (explains but does not define).
Uses Marley as a structural contrast (regret too late).

exam.q: Practice: write a paragraph on how Dickens presents the future.
exam.tip: Link future to choice and hope.

mistakes.r: It explains him; Belle shows he made choices.

summary: A full grade 9 part (b) model essay on time, memory and regret, arguing that Dickens structures the novella around time to show that the past explains us but does not have to define our future.
